mcqs.question: Why can a component re-render even when its own props are identical to last time?
options: Because its parent re-rendered and this component isn't memoized, so React re-renders it unconditionally
Because React re-renders every component once per second by default
Because identical props always trigger a forced re-render for consistency
Because state and props are compared using deep equality by default
mcqs.explanation: React's default behavior is to re-render every non-memoized child whenever its parent re-renders, regardless of whether the child's own props changed — it doesn't check unless `React.memo` tells it to. There's no periodic re-render timer and no forced re-render on identical props.

mcqs.question: What does `useCallback` actually memoize?
options: A component's rendered output
A function reference, keeping it stable across renders when dependencies haven't changed
An expensive computed value derived from state
A component's entire prop object
mcqs.explanation: `useCallback` returns the same function identity across renders as long as its dependencies are unchanged — its main purpose is letting a `React.memo`-wrapped child actually see stable props, since a freshly-created function reference every render would otherwise defeat the shallow-equality check. `useMemo` is the one for computed values.

mcqs.question: What does list virtualization avoid, for a list far longer than the visible viewport?
options: The need for a scrollbar on the list at all
Ever re-rendering the list once it's mounted
Creating a real DOM node for every item — only rows near the visible viewport are rendered
The need for a unique `key` on each row
mcqs.explanation: Virtualization renders only the handful of rows in or near the viewport and repositions/re-populates them as the user scrolls, avoiding the memory, layout, and paint cost of thousands of off-screen DOM nodes. It still needs a scrollbar and stable keys — those requirements don't go away.

mcqs.question: In the windowing example, why is the outer container given a height of `items.length * rowHeight` even though only ~17 rows are actually rendered?
options: To preload all row data into memory ahead of scrolling
To satisfy a requirement that every list have a fixed pixel height
To allow the browser's native find-in-page feature to search unrendered rows
To give the scrollbar the correct total scrollable size, even though the DOM only holds the currently visible rows
mcqs.explanation: The full-size outer container makes the scrollbar behave as if every row exists, while the actual rendered rows — absolutely positioned inside it — are only ever the small visible window. Find-in-page in fact can't search rows that aren't in the DOM, which is one of virtualization's known trade-offs.

mcqs.question: What's the risk of wrapping every component in `React.memo` and every function in `useCallback` by default?
options: The comparison overhead can outweigh the render cost it was meant to avoid, and dependency arrays become another place to introduce stale-closure bugs
React disables memoization automatically once too many components use it
It permanently disables re-rendering for the entire application
It converts all local state into global state automatically
mcqs.explanation: Every memoization has a real cost — a comparison or a stored reference — so applying it to cheap, rarely-re-rendered components can add overhead with no measurable gain, plus the exact stale-closure risk from incomplete dependency arrays covered in the hooks topic. Measuring first is what avoids this.

mcqs.question: Why do Vue and Svelte need `React.memo`-style manual re-render skipping far less often than React?
options: Because they don't support component props at all
Because their fine-grained reactivity already tracks dependencies and skips subtrees a change doesn't affect
Because they virtualize every list automatically without any library
Because they re-render the entire application on every state change instead of per-component
mcqs.explanation: Fine-grained reactivity already knows exactly which DOM bindings depend on which value, so there's no unnecessary re-render to opt out of in the first place. Neither framework auto-virtualizes lists — that's still a userland library concern in all three ecosystems.
